meta.title: Who really said "If Mormonism is able to endure, unmodified, until it reaches the third and fourth generation, it is destined to become the greatest power the world has ever known"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not documented from Tolstoy. The line first appears in a February 1939 Improvement Era article by Thomas J. Yates — a story Andrew D. White's own account contradicts.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If Mormonism is able to endure, unmodified, until it reaches the third and fourth generation, it is destined to become the greatest power the world has ever known'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is documented only in Thomas J. Yates's February 1939 Improvement Era article — retold twice from memory, and contradicted by Andrew D. White's own published account.

answer.label: Not documented from Tolstoy — a 1939 third-hand recollection
answer.authorDates: Cornell class of 1902 · Utah electrical engineer · the first person known to put this sentence in print
answer.sourceLine: The sentence has never been traced to anything Leo Tolstoy wrote or is recorded as saying. Its earliest known appearance is Thomas J. Yates’s article in the February 1939 Improvement Era ↗, where Yates recounts a conversation he says he had at Cornell in 1900 with Andrew D. White, who was recalling a meeting with Tolstoy in 1894. White’s own published account of that meeting reads very differently.
answer.confidenceText: Documented only at third hand, and contradicted by the one firsthand published record.

source.excerpt: There have been great movements started in the past but they have died or been modified before they reached maturity. If Mormonism is able to endure, unmodified, until it reaches the third and fourth generation, it is destined to become the greatest power the world has ever known.
trail: The wording appears, exactly as it circulates today, on page 94 of the February 1939 Improvement Era ↗, whose masthead identifies it as an official organ of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The author, Thomas J. Yates, opens by saying it was in 1900, while he was a student at Cornell, that he met Andrew D. White and heard the story.

Yates stages the scene in a field, with Tolstoy pausing at the plow. White’s own published account — chapter XXXVII of his Autobiography, headed “Walks and Talks with Tolstoi—March, 1894” ↗ — puts the religion conversation indoors in Moscow, and records Tolstoy asking about the Mormons and thinking “two thirds of their religion deception.” No prediction of world-conquering power appears anywhere in it.

Leland A. Fetzer’s “Tolstoy and Mormonism,” Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought 6, no. 1 (Spring 1971) ↗ examined the Yates story directly. Fetzer found the three statements Yates attributes to Tolstoy recorded in no other source, noted that Yates wrote thirty-nine years after the conversation he was reporting, and concluded that these facts cast very serious doubt on the reliability of Yates’s account.

Wikiquote’s Leo Tolstoy page ↗ files the line under Disputed and traces it to the same source — Yates, Improvement Era, February 1939, p. 94 — noting Fetzer’s finding that Yates likely misremembered the interview and that no other contemporaneous evidence corroborates it. Quote Investigator’s Tolstoy tag ↗ has no entry on it.
source.excerptNote: These are the closing lines of a speech Yates puts in Tolstoy’s mouth. They are Yates’s 1939 recollection of White’s 1900 retelling of a conversation of 1894 — not a transcript, and not anything Tolstoy is known to have written down.
source.rightsHolder: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, publisher of the Improvement Era; the estate of Thomas J. Yates
source.rightsNote: The only text this wording can be tied to is Yates’s article in the February 1939 Improvement Era — a 1939 American periodical, so it is treated here as in copyright rather than public domain, and we have not established whether its US registration was renewed. Andrew D. White’s Autobiography (New York: The Century Co., 1905), quoted alongside it, is long out of copyright.

author.name: Thomas J. Yates
author.kicker: The man who wrote it down
author.heading: Who actually put this sentence in print
author.metaLine: Cornell class of 1902 · electrical engineer from Scipio, Utah · author of the February 1939 Improvement Era article
author.bio: Thomas J. Yates served as a Latter-day Saint missionary in the Southern States from 1895 to 1898, then left Utah for Cornell University, graduating in 1902 as an electrical engineer — details given in the Improvement Era’s own note on him. In 1900, as a student, he was introduced to Andrew Dickson White, Cornell’s first president and then US ambassador to Germany, who invited him back to talk about Mormonism; Yates says the invitation grew out of White’s conversation with Tolstoy. Nearly four decades later he published his memory of that evening, and with it the sentence that has been circulating under Tolstoy’s name ever since.

cite.sourceCitation: Thomas J. Yates, "Count Tolstoi and the 'American Religion'," The Improvement Era 42, no. 2 (February 1939): 94. copyAttribution: Widely credited to Leo Tolstoy, but no source in his own writings has been found. The line's earliest known printing is Thomas J. Yates, "Count Tolstoi and the 'American Religion'," The Improvement Era, February 1939, p. 94 — a story retold from memory in 1939 about a conversation of 1900 about a meeting of 1894. Andrew D. White's own published account of that 1894 meeting contains nothing like it. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The line is quoted constantly as Tolstoy’s, usually with no source at all. There is a source — it is just three removes from Tolstoy, and the one firsthand record of the meeting it describes says something close to the opposite.

items.why: Nothing in Tolstoy’s books, essays, letters or diaries has been shown to contain it. Wikiquote’s Tolstoy page ↗ lists it only under Disputed, attributing its origin to Yates’s 1939 article rather than to anything Tolstoy wrote, and Leland A. Fetzer’s 1971 survey in Dialogue ↗ found the statements Yates reports in no other source.

Yates presents White as his authority, but White had already published his own account. In chapter XXXVII of his Autobiography ↗ Tolstoy asks about the Mormons, thinks “two thirds of their religion deception,” and it is White — not Tolstoy — who makes the generational prediction, forecasting that once outside pressure eases the young will “split the whole body into sects and parties.”

Yates has White walking a furrow beside Tolstoy as he ploughs. White’s account of the March 1894 visit has Tolstoy coming to his rooms in Moscow — a discrepancy Fetzer flags ↗ as evidence of how far the story had drifted.

misattribution.truthLine: Treat it as a story about Thomas J. Yates’s memory, not as a statement by Tolstoy. The only firsthand published record of the conversation is White’s own ↗, and it contains no such prediction.

context.heading: How a memory became a quotation
lead: Andrew Dickson White was US minister to Russia in the early 1890s, and in March 1894 he spent several days in Moscow talking with Tolstoy. He wrote the visit up at length. In one exchange Tolstoy, who had been reading Latter-day Saint books, asks White about the Mormons, calls two thirds of their religion deception, and remarks that he would rather have a faith that claimed to dig its scriptures out of the ground than one that claimed they were let down from heaven. White answers that Mormonism cannot yet be judged, because this is its heroic period, and that the real test will come when the pressure lifts and the next generation starts asking questions.

In 1900 White told a version of that meeting to a young Utah student at Cornell. In 1939 the student, Thomas J. Yates, published what he remembered, and in his telling the generational test sits in a different mouth and points the other way: it is Tolstoy speaking, and the outcome is not fragmentation but the greatest power the world has ever known. Fetzer’s suggestion is that the two got swapped in memory — could Yates have recalled White’s own prediction and, over the years, attributed it to Tolstoy instead, simplifying it and altering its thrust? He puts it as a question rather than a finding, adding that there will never be a solution to the question of the reliability of Yates’s version. Either way, Yates’s is the version the internet inherited.
detailsBody: Fetzer’s 1971 article in Dialogue is still the standard treatment. He does not accuse Yates of inventing anything; his objection is structural. The story reached print through two long stretches of memory — White recalling 1894 in 1900, Yates recalling 1900 in 1939 — and nothing else in the record corroborates it.

Tolstoy’s genuine interest in Mormonism is not in question; White’s own pages document that he had been reading some of the movement’s books. What is missing is any evidence that he ever predicted its triumph.
context.pull: Both accounts predict a third-and-fourth-generation test. Whether one became the other is a question Fetzer says will never be settled.
